extracted.intended_audience: Federal agency NEPA practitioners, counsel, and decisionmakers responsible for determining NEPA applicability, scope, level of review, and significance
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and procedural standards for determining whether NEPA applies to a proposed activity or decision, how to define the scope of action and connected actions, selecting the appropriate level of NEPA review (CE/EA/EIS), and applying context and intensity factors in significance determinations under revised §1501.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold determination — determine whether NEPA applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must determine whether NEPA applies to a proposed activity or decision as a threshold matter (move of paragraph (a) of 40 CFR 1501.1 to new §1501.3(a), titled 'Applicability').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry into whether NEPA applies is a component of determining the level of NEPA review; CEQ consolidated the steps into one regulatory section to improve clarity and consistency with section 106 of NEPA. Agencies have flexibility to consider the factors in any order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and 'another provision of Federal law' factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider whether the activity is 'exempted from NEPA by law' or is governed by 'another provision of Federal law' when assessing whether NEPA applies (moving and aligning text from 40 CFR 1501.1(a)(1) and (a)(2) to §1501.3(a)(1) and (2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added the word 'Federal' to avoid confusion that non-Federal legal requirements can override NEPA; interpretation is informed by the Supremacy Clause and case law. CEQ rejects treating state, tribal, or local law as overriding Federal law for NEPA applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on 'functional equivalence' factor
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ removed the phrase 'or is otherwise fulfilled' and proposed removal of the functional equivalence factor from the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The removal means agencies should not treat functional equivalence as a regulatory factor in assessing NEPA applicability; this change was made for clarity as discussed in section II.C.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and fundamental conflict with other Federal law
rubrics_metrics.description: If NEPA's application would present a clear and fundamental conflict with another provision of Federal law, section 106(a) provides that 'an agency is not required to prepare an environmental document with respect to a proposed agency action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ disagrees that agencies must apply principles of statutory interpretation before invoking section 106(a); where a clear and fundamental conflict exists with Federal law, NEPA does not require an environmental document. Commenters' distinctions involving State/tribal/local laws do not change this Federal-law-focused rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not add a separate 'impossibility' factor
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ proposed then declined to include a separate factor addressing circumstances where statutory provisions make compliance with NEPA impossible (proposed paragraph (a)(3) was duplicative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the proposed 'impossible' factor duplicated paragraph (a)(2), CEQ removed it to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Federal action as a factor in applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the activity or decision is a 'major Federal action' is a factor agencies should consider when determining if NEPA applies (redesignation of paragraph (a)(4) to §1501.3(a)(3) and cross-reference to definition §1508.1(w)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ considers determining whether an action is a major Federal action to be a component of NEPA applicability; agencies may consider this factor in any order with other applicability factors. CEQ did not include the proposed cross-reference as an exclusion from the definition in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final agency action (APA) as a stand-alone factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proposed activity or decision is a final agency action under the Administrative Procedure Act is a stand-alone factor in assessing NEPA applicability (added as §1501.3(a)(4)(i); final rule phrased as '[w]hether the proposed activity or decision is not a final agency action').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor requires agencies to evaluate whether the proposed action would be a final agency action if ultimately taken; CEQ added 'not' to align with section 106(a)(1) and parallelism among factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-discretionary actions as an applicability factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-discretionary actions are a stand-alone factor in determining NEPA applicability (moved to §1501.3(a)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although non-discretionary actions are excluded from the definition of 'major Federal action,' CEQ highlights this category as a component of NEPA applicability because Congress did so; agencies may exclude non-discretionary components from analysis when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude non-discretionary components from NEPA analysis where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where some components of an action are non-discretionary but others are discretionary, agencies can exclude consideration of the non-discretionary components from NEPA analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This circumstance affects the appropriate scope of analysis rather than applicability (e.g., statute mandates a decision once criteria are met but agency has flexibility in how to meet them — agency exercises discretion on aspects and can analyze alternatives/effects for those aspects). CEQ included a cross-reference to scope in paragraph (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope determination — consider connected actions and avoid segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must determine the scope of the proposed action and its potential effects, including consideration of connected actions (moved from 40 CFR 1501.9(e) into §1501.3(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connected actions are closely related Federal activities or decisions that should be considered in a single NEPA document; CEQ moved specific types of connected actions into §1501.3(b)(1)-(3). The longstanding doctrine prohibits improper segmentation of Federal actions (citing case law such as Fath v. Texas DOT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat non-Federal actions as connected actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Connected actions are limited to Federal activities/decisions; non-Federal actions have long been excluded from connected actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose is to prevent segmentation by the Federal Government; including non-Federal actions as connected actions would be inconsistent with the doctrine and unsettled NEPA implementation (citing Sierra Club v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public engagement and scoping mechanisms to inform scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must use, as appropriate, the public engagement and scoping mechanisms in §§1501.9 and 1502.4 to inform the consideration of the scope of the proposed action and determination of the level of NEPA review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added this to clarify the connection between scope, scoping, and public engagement and to assist agencies in determining scope and level of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider only reasonably foreseeable effects in scope and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to consider 'effects' as defined in the regulations, i.e., reasonably foreseeable effects; CEQ deleted the word 'potential' before 'effects' to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are not required to consider speculative or non-reasonably-foreseeable effects; the definition of 'effect' in the regulations limits this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-segmentation rule — cannot term temporary if not temporary or split action to avoid significant effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies 'shall not term an action temporary that is not temporary in fact or segment an action into smaller component parts to avoid significant effects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ revised language from proposed paragraph (d)(2)(vi) and moved it to §1501.3(b) to address segmentation in the paragraph on scope rather than intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of NEPA review and use of reliable data sources (CE/EA/EIS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (c) redesignates the three levels of review—categorical exclusions (CEs), environmental assessments (EAs), and environmental impact statements (EISs)—and incorporates section 106(b)(3) directing agencies to rely on reliable data sources when determining the appropriate level of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ requires agencies to make use of any reliable data source in considering whether to apply a CE; a decision based on unreliable data would likely be inconsistent with reasoned decision making. Section 106(b)(3)(B) states agencies 'are not required to undertake new scientific or technical research' except in identified circumstances. CEQ may provide further guidance separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of section 106(b)(3) to CE determinations — limits on new research
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are not required to undertake new scientific or technical research for CE determinations outside the circumstances identified in section 106(b)(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making the section 106(b)(3) standard applicable to CE determinations preserves CE efficiency and avoids creating an undefined obligation to undertake new research for CE decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance determination — consider context and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider the context of an action and the intensity of the effects when determining whether a proposed action's effects are significant (redesignation and restoration of 'context' and 'intensity' in §1501.3(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ restored and expanded these factors from the 1978 regulations because they assist agencies in focusing review on critical factors for significance determinations; CEQ moved language about beneficial/adverse effects and segmentation to the end of paragraph (d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context factors — geographic area, unique/sensitive resources, and communities with environmental justice concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies 'shall' analyze the significance of an action in several contexts and 'should' consider characteristics of the geographic area, proximity to unique or sensitive resources, Tribal sacred sites, and communities with environmental justice concerns (replaces 'vulnerable communities').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ included examples and encourages consideration of global, national, regional, and local contexts as appropriate depending on the scope of the action. CEQ declined to define 'geographic area' or 'unique or sensitive resources' and removed the modifier 'relevant' before 'geographic area' to avoid implying a different analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider global, national, regional, and local contexts as appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are encouraged to consider potential global, national, regional, and local contexts when assessing significance, depending on the scope and reasonably foreseeable effects of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ does not require agencies to evaluate all four contexts for every action; agencies should determine appropriate contexts based on the action's scope and anticipated reasonably foreseeable effects. Examples illustrate when global or regional contexts may be pertinent (e.g., migratory species, transboundary watershed) and when local context suffices (e.g., office building on previously developed land).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity factors — analyze degree of effects in relation to listed factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze the intensity of effects in light of the list of factors (the intensity factors) as applicable to the proposed action and in relation to one another when determining significance (reinstatement of 'intensity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensity factors inform whether an effect is significant; CEQ reframed 'degree' back to 'intensity' because the concept guides significance determinations. The regulation assumes 'effect' means reasonably foreseeable effects, so repeating that phrase in each factor is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on adverse effects for EIS requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects may be beneficial or adverse, but 'only actions with significant adverse effects require an [EIS].' A significant adverse effect may exist even if the agency considers the overall balance of effects to be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision distinguishes evaluating whether an adverse effect is significant from weighing overall benefits against adverse effects to conclude no significant effects. Agencies should also consider duration of effects (e.g., short-term adverse but long-term beneficial) in significance determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain 'adverse' and rely on defined 'effect' meaning (reasonably foreseeable)
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ retains 'adverse' in intensity-factor language and declines to insert 'reasonably foreseeable' repeatedly because 'effect' is defined to mean reasonably foreseeable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ rejected editorial suggestions to alter phrasing that could suggest agencies must consider speculative scenarios; the intensity factors apply only to reasonably foreseeable adverse effects by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation and mitigated FONSI documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency determines that a proposed action would not have a significant effect because of the implementation of mitigation, the agency must document its finding in a mitigated FONSI (addressed in §1501.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declined to address mitigation's role in paragraph (d) because §1501.6 already clarifies the need for a mitigated FONSI when mitigation forms the basis for a finding of no significant impact.
